events.text: A frontier garrison holds an archery contest: a copper coin hung from a willow at a hundred paces, and a purse for whoever splits it.

ok.log: Your arrow takes the coin off its string. The garrison captain buys you a cup of tea and asks where you learned.

fail.log: Your arrow sings past the coin and sticks in the willow. The soldiers are kind about it, which is worse.

effects.log: You watch the old scouts draw and release without seeming to aim. Something in it stays with you.

events.text: Wolves on a winter road, six of them, circling at the edge of your firelight. You have a bow and a quiver.

ok.log: One arrow in the dark. The pack scatters without its leader, and you sleep with the bow across your knees.

fail.log: The arrow goes wide and the pack comes in. You drive them off with a burning branch and bleeding arms.

choices.text: Build the fire higher and wait for dawn

effects.log: A long night. At dawn the wolves are gone and so is half your firewood.

events.text: A big man is shaking down a noodle seller in the market. He has a sabre; you have one finger and know where to put it.

ok.log: One touch under the collarbone and he stands there like a statue, sabre raised, while the whole market laughs. You leave him that way until noon.

fail.log: You find the point a finger's width too high. He finds your jaw with his fist.

choices.text: Pay the noodle seller's debt instead

effects.log: You pay. The big man leaves. The noodle seller gives you free noodles for a month.

events.text: A carter lies bleeding in the road from a bandit's cut, and the physician is an hour away. You know the points that close a wound.

ok.log: Three points, pressed in order. The bleeding slows to a trickle, and he is alive when the physician comes running.

fail.log: You press the points you know. It is not enough, but you held his hand until the end, and his family remembers that.

effects.log: You ride as if the horse were on fire. The physician makes it in time, barely.

events.text: Three thugs block an alley, one with a club, two with knives. Two short blades leave your sleeves before they finish their threat.

ok.log: Two blades, three men, four seconds. You take the club as a souvenir and their purse as a fee.

fail.log: Two blades are not enough hands for three men. You get out of the alley; so do they, with your purse.

effects.log: You walk backwards, blades out, until the street. They do not follow.

events.text: A travelling troupe has lost its sword dancer to a broken ankle. They have seen you practise, and they are desperate.

ok.log: Two blades flashing in the lantern light, and a crowd that forgets to breathe. The troupe begs you to stay.

fail.log: You cut the troupe's banner in half. They pay you anyway, mostly to make you stop.

choices.text: Lend them a practice pair of blades instead

effects.log: Their understudy dances with the borrowed practice pair. One comes back a little chipped.

events.text: A drunk swordsman in the teahouse reads your poem aloud in a silly voice. Your fan is already open in your hand.

choices.text: Answer with the fan's iron ribs

ok.log: The fan closes on his wrist, his sword clatters to the floor, and you finish the poem for him. The teahouse applauds.

fail.log: He is faster than he is drunk. You leave with your fan in two pieces and your poem unfinished.

choices.text: Write a poem about him on the wall

effects.log: Eight lines. The teahouse keeps them on the wall for years. He never comes back.

events.text: A young master of a rich house wants your iron fan. He names a price that would buy a horse, and then another.

effects.log: You sell the fan and buy a better one, and a horse. He is seen in the capital a year later, trying to open it with both hands.
A gentleman's fan is not for sale. He is offended, then impressed, then tells everyone.

events.text: At the temple fair a showman dares anyone to knock a cup off a post with a weight on a rope: whoever does it wins a string of coins.

ok.log: The meteor hammer takes the cup off the post without touching the post. The showman pays, and asks you to stay away from his stall.

fail.log: The weight takes the cup, the post, and the showman's hat. You pay for the hat.

effects.log: A six-year-old does it on the third try. The showman looks ill.

events.text: A horse thief gallops past with a farmer's mare, far too fast to catch on foot. Your chain is coiled at your belt.

ok.log: The chain wraps his arm and the weight pulls him out of the saddle. The mare stops by herself and looks at him.

fail.log: You catch the saddle instead of the thief, and the mare drags you a hundred paces before the chain lets go.

effects.log: The farmer watches his mare disappear. So do you.

events.text: Half a village is sick, and the physician is baffled. You taste the well water and know the poison by its bitterness, because you have made it.

ok.log: Three herbs and a night at the cauldron. By morning the sick are sitting up. Nobody asks how you knew.

fail.log: Your antidote is close but not right. The physician builds on it, and the village recovers a week late.

effects.log: Knowing the poison would mean explaining how. You leave the village the next morning.

events.text: A quiet woman with green-stained fingernails sits down at your table. 'Ten Thousand Poison Valley has watched your work. We would like to show you a recipe nobody outside the valley knows.'

effects.log: She writes it on a leaf that dissolves after you read it. You will never forget it, and you will never be quite trusted again.
She nods, as if she expected it, and leaves a vial on the table. You do not open it.

events.text: A dozen bandits step out of the trees around your cart. A dozen is too many for a blade. It is not too many for a voice.

ok.log: The Lion's Roar knocks leaves off the trees and bandits off their feet. Three of them are still running at sunset.

fail.log: The roar cracks halfway out. They laugh, and then they rob you.

effects.log: Silver is cheaper than blood. They let you pass, whistling.

events.text: A blind qin master challenges you to a duel of sound on a bridge at midnight: two instruments, no blades, the first to break the other's note loses.

ok.log: Your note holds. His string snaps. He laughs with delight and teaches you a tune nobody else alive knows.

fail.log: His note goes through you like cold water. You wake on the bridge at dawn with a terrible headache and a new respect for music.

effects.log: He plays alone until the stars fade. It is the best music you will ever hear.

events.text: A crowd in the inn does not believe a sword can cut from across a room. Someone lights a candle on the far table and looks at you.

ok.log: A flick of the wrist. The flame goes out across the room, and the top of the candle slides off a breath later. Nobody speaks for a while.

fail.log: The flame flickers. The candle stays whole. Someone coughs politely and the conversation moves on.

effects.log: A master does not perform for drinks. You finish your tea.

events.text: The leader of a dock gang has heard you can cut from a distance and has decided it is a trick. He has twenty men to prove it.

ok.log: You cut the belt off him from ten paces. His trousers fall down in front of twenty men, and the dock gang finds another leader.

fail.log: The qi is there but not enough of it. Twenty men are enough of them.

effects.log: You walk away. The story that follows you is not the one you would have chosen.

events.text: A swordsman with a famous blade, three hundred years old and never notched, wants to test it against your sword aura.

ok.log: Light meets steel. The famous blade comes away in two pieces, and its owner stares at the hilt for a long time before he bows.

fail.log: Your aura flickers at the wrong moment. His blade holds; yours does not. You pay for a new one.

choices.text: Refuse: the blade is too fine to risk

effects.log: He is relieved, and grateful, and tells everyone you spared his sword out of respect.

events.text: A sheer cliff above the river, where the great masters of old carved their names with their swords. There is room for one more.

effects.log: Three strokes of light into the rock. Boatmen point at it for a hundred years.
Eight lines nobody can read from the river, cut a finger deep. You tell no one which cliff.

events.text: A challenger finds you at the hot spring, unarmed and in your bathing robe. He thinks this is clever.

ok.log: You raise two fingers. His sword falls in three pieces, and his belt in two. He leaves holding up his trousers, and the murim tells the story for a century.

fail.log: The sword in your heart is not yet quite a sword. You lose some skin and most of your sleeve.

choices.text: Ask him to wait while you dress

effects.log: He waits, mortified. By the time you are dressed he has apologised and gone.

events.text: A young prodigy kneels in the snow outside your gate for three days, begging to understand how a sword can be in the heart.

effects.log: Ten years, and a thousand cups of tea. They never quite understand it. Neither, you admit, did you until you taught it.

choices.text: Send them away with one sentence

effects.log: 'Stop looking for the sword.' They leave confused. Twenty years later a letter arrives: they understood.

events.text: Your breathing has been slow and deep for so many years that your face has forgotten to age. An old friend at the market does not recognise you until you speak.

choices.text: Tell them it is the method

effects.log: They want to learn it at once. You explain that it took decades. They lose interest.

choices.text: Say it must be the mountain air

effects.log: They move to the mountains the next spring. The air does nothing for them.

events.text: In the still hours before dawn, the slow tide of your method carries you somewhere quiet, and you see the shape of the next gate as plainly as a door.

effects.log: You sit until the sun is high. The door is still there when you open your eyes, a little closer.

choices.text: Let the tide carry you back

effects.log: You wake rested in a way you have not been since childhood.

events.text: Two monks on the road stop dead and listen to your breathing. Then they bow to you, which is not something monks do to laymen.

effects.log: 'Your breath carries the sutra,' says the older one. 'We have not heard it outside the temple in thirty years.'
Three people breathing by the roadside. Carts go around you. It is the best hour of your year.

events.text: A stranger leaves a manual on your table and walks out. It is a demonic art, and it is very, very good. Your pure scripture will not survive reading it.

effects.log: It burns green. You feel lighter for weeks.
You read it in one night. Your breathing is never quite clear again, and you are never quite as weak.

events.text: You come out of a deep breathing session to find the whole street looking at you. Apparently you were howling.

effects.log: The dogs of the street answer you. The neighbours do not speak to you for a month, which is restful.
Nobody believes you. Nobody says so.

events.text: A thunderstorm breaks over the mountain, and your wild method pulls at you like a leash. The old masters trained in weather like this. Most of them survived.

ok.log: Lightning walks the ridge around you and your energy roars with it. You come down at dawn, singed and grinning.

fail.log: The storm wins. You come down at dawn with your eyebrows gone and a new respect for the old masters.

choices.text: Breathe with it from the doorway

effects.log: Thunder in the chest, rain on the face, the method humming. Enough.
